questions.q: What does Databricks say a data lakehouse combines?

options.t: A message queue and a key-value store, so events and lookups share one engine
options.why: A lakehouse combines data lakes and data warehouses.

options.t: The benefits of data lakes and data warehouses
An on-premises Hadoop cluster and a cloud backup of its files
options.why: A lakehouse combines lake and warehouse benefits on open files in cloud storage.

options.t: A relational database and a separate copy of it for reporting
options.why: The point is one copy of data, not a second reporting copy.

questions.explain: A data lakehouse combines the benefits of data lakes and data warehouses: open, direct access to data in cloud object storage plus reliable BI and ML on the same data.

questions.q: Which component gives Databricks tables ACID transactions and schema enforcement?

options.t: Unity Catalog, which records every write in its audit log
options.why: Unity Catalog governs access; Delta Lake provides ACID transactions.

options.t: Photon, the engine that executes every write in a transaction
options.why: Photon is a query engine; Delta Lake provides transactions.

options.t: Delta Lake
Lakeflow Jobs, which retries writes until they succeed
options.why: Jobs orchestrate tasks; Delta Lake provides transactions.

questions.explain: On Databricks the lakehouse rests on Apache Spark (compute), Delta Lake (ACID, schema enforcement) and Unity Catalog (governance).

questions.q: A table is created on Databricks without naming a format. What is it?

options.t: A Delta table
A Parquet table without a transaction log
options.why: Delta is the default for every table unless otherwise specified.

options.t: A CSV table, until a format is chosen later
options.why: Delta is the default.

options.t: An Iceberg table, the default format since 2025
options.why: Delta is the default.

questions.explain: Unless otherwise specified, every table on Databricks is a Delta Lake table.

questions.q: On Azure Databricks, where does classic compute run?

options.t: In the Azure Databricks account, in a network boundary per workspace
options.why: That describes serverless compute.

options.t: In the control plane, next to the web application
options.why: The control plane holds backend services; classic compute runs in your subscription.

options.t: In your Azure subscription, inside the workspace's virtual network
In a shared multi-tenant cluster that all customers use
options.why: Classic compute runs in your own subscription.

questions.explain: Classic compute runs in the classic compute plane in your Azure subscription; serverless runs in a serverless compute plane in the Azure Databricks account, in your region.

questions.q: Where do the web application and backend services of Azure Databricks run?

options.t: In your subscription's managed resource group, on VMs you pay for
options.why: The control plane lives in the Azure Databricks account.

options.t: On the driver node of each cluster
options.why: The control plane is a separate set of services.

options.t: In your ADLS Gen2 account, as static files
options.why: The control plane runs in the Azure Databricks account.

options.t: In the control plane, in the Azure Databricks account

questions.explain: The control plane (backend services, the web application) lives in the Azure Databricks account, not in your subscription.

questions.q: Which statement about Unity Catalog metastores is correct?

options.t: Each workspace must have its own metastore, never shared
options.why: A metastore can be attached to several workspaces in the same region.

options.t: A metastore can be attached to several workspaces in the same region
One metastore serves workspaces in every region of the account
options.why: Metastores are per region.

options.t: Metastores are created inside each workspace by workspace admins
options.why: The metastore is managed at the account level.

questions.explain: The account manages Unity Catalog metastores; a metastore can be attached to several workspaces in the same region, which then share one view of the data and its access controls.

questions.q: Which compute is versionless, always on the latest runtime?

options.t: Classic all-purpose compute with autoscaling enabled
options.why: Classic compute runs the runtime you choose.

options.t: Classic job compute pinned to an LTS runtime
options.why: That runtime is chosen and pinned.

options.t: Serverless compute
A pool of idle instances
options.why: Pools serve classic compute with a chosen runtime.

questions.explain: Serverless compute is versionless: always the latest runtime.

questions.q: A nightly ETL job runs on a shared all-purpose cluster. What does the documentation say about that?

options.t: It is billed at the all-purpose rate; Databricks doesn't recommend all-purpose compute for production jobs
It is the recommended pattern, because the cluster is already running for interactive users
options.why: Databricks doesn't recommend all-purpose compute for production jobs.

options.t: It is free, because all-purpose clusters are billed only for notebook commands
options.why: All-purpose compute is billed, at a different rate from job compute.

options.t: It can't run at all, because jobs refuse all-purpose clusters
options.why: Jobs can use all-purpose compute; it just isn't recommended for production.

questions.explain: On Azure, job compute and all-purpose compute are billed at different rates, and Databricks does not recommend all-purpose compute for production jobs.

questions.q: Thirty business users run ad hoc SQL and dashboards at unpredictable times. Which compute does Databricks point to?

options.t: A classic SQL warehouse that runs all day with a fixed size
options.why: Serverless suits many concurrent ad hoc users, scaling quickly without idling.

options.t: A shared all-purpose cluster with a high autoscaling maximum
options.why: SQL and BI users are served by SQL warehouses.

options.t: One job compute cluster per user, started on demand
options.why: Job compute runs jobs; SQL users use warehouses.

options.t: A serverless SQL warehouse

questions.explain: Serverless SQL warehouses (Photon, Predictive IO, Intelligent Workload Management) start in about 2-6 seconds and scale fast; they are Databricks' choice for many concurrent BI and ad hoc users.

questions.q: On Azure, what do you pay for when running classic compute?

options.t: Only DBUs, because Databricks covers the virtual machines
options.why: With classic compute you pay Azure for the VMs as well as DBUs.

options.t: The virtual machines, and DBUs based on the instance chosen
Only the virtual machines; DBUs apply to serverless only
options.why: Classic compute is billed in DBUs as well as VMs.

options.t: A flat monthly fee per workspace, whatever is run
options.why: Billing is VMs plus DBUs per second.

questions.explain: Azure Databricks bills for the VMs provisioned in clusters and for DBUs based on the instance selected, per second; with serverless, only DBUs are billed.

questions.q: Which access mode does Databricks recommend by default for clusters shared by many users?

options.t: Dedicated, assigned to one user or group
options.why: Dedicated is for what standard doesn't support.

options.t: No isolation shared, the legacy mode for older runtimes
options.why: That is a legacy configuration, not recommended.

options.t: Standard (formerly shared), isolated by Lakeguard
Single node, so users can't affect each other
options.why: Single node is a cluster size choice, not an access mode.

questions.explain: Standard access mode (formerly shared) lets many users share compute, isolated by Lakeguard; it is Databricks' default recommendation. Dedicated (formerly single user) is for what standard doesn't support.

questions.q: Which workload needs dedicated access mode rather than standard?

options.t: A SQL notebook reading Unity Catalog tables
options.why: Standard access mode supports that.

options.t: A Python notebook writing Delta tables
options.why: Standard access mode supports that.

options.t: A scheduled notebook task that runs a MERGE
options.why: Standard access mode supports that.

options.t: A GPU workload using the ML runtime

questions.explain: Standard access mode doesn't support the ML runtime, GPUs, R, Spark Submit tasks or some SparkContext APIs; use dedicated for those.

questions.q: Which runtime choice does Databricks recommend for production jobs on classic compute?

options.t: An LTS (long-term support) runtime
The newest beta runtime, to get fixes first
options.why: Production jobs should use an LTS version.

options.t: The oldest runtime still listed, because it is the most tested
options.why: Choose a supported LTS version.

options.t: Any runtime, because jobs always upgrade to the latest automatically
options.why: Classic compute runs the runtime you pick; choose LTS for production.

questions.explain: Choose the latest runtime for all-purpose compute and an LTS version for production jobs.

questions.q: What does Photon change for a workload?

options.t: It speeds up SQL, DataFrames, ETL and Delta writes, with no code changes
It requires rewriting PySpark code in its own API before it runs faster
options.why: Photon needs no code changes.

options.t: It replaces Delta Lake as the storage format for faster reads
options.why: Photon is an engine, not a storage format.

options.t: It is only used for streaming queries in real-time mode
options.why: Photon speeds up SQL, DataFrames, ETL and Delta writes generally.

questions.explain: Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine, on by default, that speeds up SQL, DataFrames, ETL and Delta writes, most for long queries on large data, with no code changes.

questions.q: A pool keeps idle instances ready for clusters. What is charged for those idle instances?

options.t: Full DBUs and VM cost, as if a cluster were running on them
options.why: No DBUs are charged for idle pool instances.

options.t: No DBUs; the cloud provider still bills the VMs
Nothing at all, from Databricks or Azure
options.why: Azure still bills the VMs.

options.t: Half the DBU rate, as a standby charge
options.why: No DBUs are charged for idle pool instances.

questions.explain: Pools keep idle instances ready to cut start-up and autoscaling time; no DBUs are charged for idle pool instances, but the cloud provider still bills the VMs.

questions.q: Which task type needs classic job compute rather than serverless?

options.t: A notebook task
options.why: Databricks recommends serverless jobs compute for notebook tasks.

options.t: A Python wheel task
options.why: Databricks recommends serverless jobs compute for wheel tasks.

options.t: A JAR task
A SQL task
options.why: SQL tasks run on a SQL warehouse, ideally serverless.

questions.explain: Recommended compute: serverless jobs for notebook, Python script and wheel tasks; a serverless SQL warehouse for SQL tasks; a serverless pipeline for pipelines. JAR and Spark Submit need classic jobs compute.

questions.q: What can an admin-defined compute policy do?

options.t: Grant SELECT on tables to users of the policy
options.why: Data privileges are Unity Catalog grants, not compute policies.

options.t: Encrypt traffic between worker nodes
options.why: That is a separate security setting.

options.t: Move clusters into another Azure region automatically
options.why: Policies constrain configuration; they don't move clusters.

options.t: Limit what users can create, such as maximum cost per cluster

questions.explain: Compute policies limit what users can create: fixed or hidden settings, cluster counts, maximum cost per cluster, required libraries; everyone gets the Personal Compute policy by default.

questions.q: Which are limitations of serverless notebooks and jobs that might lead a team to use classic compute?

options.t: Only availableNow and Once streaming triggers
No JAR or Spark Submit tasks
No access to Unity Catalog tables
options.why: Serverless is available in Unity Catalog workspaces and reads their tables.

options.t: No Python notebooks
options.why: Serverless runs Python notebooks.

options.t: No Delta Lake writes
options.why: Serverless writes Delta tables.

questions.explain: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only AvailableNow and Once triggers, and JAR and Spark Submit tasks need classic jobs compute.
